and the “resulting loss of confidence in the impartiality of the institutions” which Article 48(3) of the Basic Regulation
intended to counteract.
3. The Appellant has raised the objection against the relevant member of the CPVO Board of Appeal
66. The Appellant has raised the Objection against the Chairperson alone in this case. The Appellant asserts that it
is correct to raise the partiality objection against the Chairperson in this case as, amongst other things, the
Chairperson is “a legally qualified member of the Board of Appeal” who is responsible for ensuring that appeal
proceedings are carried out in accordance with the legal requirements concerning due process which include “the
right to a fair trial” and “the equality of arms of the parties”. In this case, the Appellant states that the Chairperson
“allowed or did not prevent” the Board of Appeal from discussing facts and asking questions before the Oral Hearing
with just one of the parties, and by doing so put just one of the parties in a position informed of the relevant
individual circumstances. The Appellant states that in this case, the Chairperson is responsible for ensuring situations
do not arise whereby one party is not informed of important issues before an Oral Hearing is scheduled to take
place, particularly where that situation is “not based on human error”. The Appellant submits that the Chairperson
“had the possibility at several times to ensure that the Appellant was also informed” of the issues to be discussed
at the Oral Hearing but “he did not do that”. According to the Appellant, the Chairperson would have allowed the
Appellant to participate in an oral hearing, while knowing that the Appellant was deprived of relevant information
“Colloquially speaking: the chairman would have let the Appellant run into the open knife.” The Appellant states
that it is “highly unlikely” that the Board’s Technical Questions would have been sent to the CPVO, and the CPVO
would have submitted its response, without the Chairperson’s knowledge as the Technically Qualified Member of
the Board of Appeal would have needed the Chairperson’s approval before taking action. Nonetheless, even if the
Chairperson did not know that the Board’s Technical Questions had been sent out to the CPVO and other parties,
and/or that the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs had been received by the Board of Appeal, the Chairperson could
and should have: found out that a matter of this gravity had occurred, informed the parties, and taken appropriate
measures, but the Chairperson “did not do that.”
67. The CPVO rejects this plea and the related lines of argument.
Findings of the Board
68. As a preliminary remark, and whilst remaining cognizant of the clear differences between the CPVO Board of
Appeal and the EU Courts of Law, and other Boards of Appeal, the Alternate Board recalls that Articles 6(1) of the
European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and Article 47 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European
Union (CFR), are generally recognised as binding standards for proceedings before, for example, the EPO Boards of
Appeal (see, for example, Case T 1627/09 of 10 October 2013 ECLI:EP:BA:2013:T162709.20131010). As such,
there should be very strict observance of the requirement for impartiality (see Case Law of the EPO Boards of Appeal
Section III, Part J, Paragraph 1.2). The Alternate Board further notes that, when carrying out their duties, Boards
of Appeal should have regard to, amongst other provisions, Article 47 of the CFR, (see Judgment of the General
Court of 20 September 2019, Germany v European Chemicals Agency, T-755/17, EU:T:2019:647, paragraph 57)
including the general legal order.
69. Given the general legal order, the similarities which exist between the CPVO Board of Appeal and other Boards
of Appeal, and given the importance of maintaining the credibility and trust which exists between the CPVO Board
of Appeal and its stakeholders, the Alternate Board notes that observance of the requirement for impartiality by the
members of the CPVO Board of Appeal is of very high importance. As such, and consistent with the principle of
good administration which requires, amongst other things, that relevant bodies examine “carefully and impartially”
all the relevant facts of a case (Judgment of the General Court, 3 October 2019, BASF v European Chemicals Agency,
T-805/17, EU:T:2019:723, paragraph 57), and in line with Article 15(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the
European Union (“TFEU”) concerning openness and transparency in the work of EU agencies and bodies, the
Alternate Board finds that it is incumbent on the CPVO Board of Appeal to ensure, insofar as it is relevant to the
CPVO Board of Appeal affairs, that justice and adherence to the principle of good administration, are not merely
done, they are seen to be done.
70. As regards to objections brought by parties pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation, the Alternate Board
notes the following. First, members of the CPVO Board of Appeal are a priori presumed to be impartial. Second, the
burden-of-proof resides with those parties who raise an objection. Third, it is incumbent on those parties who raise
an objection to ensure that the objection itself is sufficiently reasoned and substantiated. In this regard the Alternate
Board notes that it is settled case-law that the facts must be capable of supporting and substantiating a suspicion
9 / 13

of partiality, in order for an objection concerning partiality to be upheld. If, for example, there are legitimate reasons
which validate the manner appeal proceedings have been conducted in the past, a party’s suspicion of partiality
based on the conduct of the appeal proceedings cannot be regarded as substantiated sufficiently or at all, and the
objection cannot be upheld (see to that effect CPVO Board of Appeal Procedural Decision of 15 May 2012, Ralf
Schräder v CPVO relating to Variety denomination Sumost 02, (“Sumost 02 Objection Decision”) (paragraphs 60-
67) and OHIM/EU IPO Boards of Appeal Cases T 0355/13 of 18 November 2015
(ECLI:EP:BA:2015:T035513.20151118) and T 1028/96 of 15 September 1999
(ECLI:EP:BA:1999:T102896.19990915).
71. The Alternate Board therefore finds it necessary to assess the evidence relied on by the Appellant to determine
whether, amongst other things, the facts are capable and sufficient to substantiate and support a reasonable
suspicion of partiality.
72. As regards the communication of 29 April 2022, the Alternate Board notes the following points.
73. First, the communication is not an instruction and does not contain an instruction. The communication is a
request to the Registry for certain action to be taken, without specifying how that action should be taken in practice.
More specifically, it is a request for the Registry to “provide [the Board’s Technical Questions] questions” to the
relevant parties. It therefore follows that the Appellant’s assertions that, for example, this communication: (1)
contained “instructions” that the Board’s Technical Questions should not be forwarded to the Appellant; and/or (2)
that the communication constituted an “instruction” to the Registry to send certain technical questions to “only one
party [in the appeal proceedings]” – cannot be sufficiently supported or substantiated by the facts.
74. Second, the communication does not mention the Appellant, and does not state whether the Board’s Technical
Questions should be provided to the Appellant or not. The email states that the Board of Appeal wishes to raise
certain questions to be “dealt with during the [Oral Hearing]”. It is sent in reply to the communication of 15 April
2022 containing the summons to the Oral Hearing, and which therefore includes the contact details of the parties
to the proceedings – including the Appellant’s. It therefore follows that the Appellant’s assertions that this
communication should be interpreted as a deliberate act intended to exclude or prevent the Appellant from receiving
the Board’s Technical Questions and, as meaning, for example, that: (1) the Board’s Technical Questions should not
be “forwarded to the Appellant”; (2) “it was…not planned to make the [Board’s Technical Questions] available to
the Appellant”; (3) this communication confirms that “it was not planned” for the Appellant to be included in the
discussions before the Oral Hearing; that it was planned that “[the Board’s Technical Questions] should be discussed
directly in the oral hearing, without the Appellant being given the opportunity to prepare well for it”; (4) that the
Chairperson purposefully “allowed or did not prevent” the Board of Appeal from discussing facts and asking
questions before the Oral Hearing with just one of the parties and by doing so intentionally put on of the parties in
a better informed position than the other; and/or (5) that the Chairperson intended that the Board’s Technical
Questions were communicated to certain parties in a non bona fide manner so as to assist the CPVO and the
Examination office to prepare for the Oral Hearing, and/or to “put [answers] into the [CPVO’s] mouth” and/or to
exclude the Appellant from preparing answers to these questions – cannot be sufficiently supported or substantiated
by the facts.
75. Third, the communication was sent by the Technically Qualified Member. It was not sent by the Chairperson,
nor was the communication sent in the name of the Chairperson or the members of the Board of Appeal. The
Alternate Board notes, in this regard, and amongst other things, the complimentary close, sender name, and
signature block contained within the email. Moreover, the Alternate Board also notes, in this regard, the legal and
factual context within which this communication was sent.
76. In appeal cases before the CPVO Board of Appeal, a chairperson is legally required to assign the examination of
the appeal to one of the members as rapporteur, which “may include, where appropriate, the taking of evidence”
(Article 11(3) of the Proceedings Regulation). A chairperson may, therefore, appoint a technically qualified member
of the CPVO Board of Appeal to act as rapporteur and assign examination to the technically qualified member.
However, in those cases where a technically qualified member wishes to obtain certain evidence, it is incumbent
upon the technically qualified member, the Registry, and other relevant individuals, to obtain the Chairperson’s
express authorisation, including any clarification of an instruction, before taking any relevant action to ensure,
amongst other things, EU law is strictly adhered to. In this case, the Alternate Board notes that there was no
authorisation or instruction from the Chairperson to exclude the Appellant in the communications concerning the
scheduled Oral Hearing, or for the Registry not to provide the Board’s Technical Questions to the Appellant, and
that no such authorisation or instruction can be inferred. The Alternate Board further notes that the evidence in this
10 / 13

regard, namely the absence of authorisation and instruction from the Chairperson, cannot be regarded as evidence
giving rise to a reasonable suspicion of partiality. Given these points, the Alternate Board finds that, contrary to the
Appellant’s assertions, the communication of 29 April 2022 cannot be regarded as giving rise to a reasonable
suspicion of partiality on the part of the Chairperson, and that any purported suspicion of partiality cannot be
sufficiently supported or substantiated by the underlying facts.
77. Given the above, the Alternate Board finds that, the communication of 29 April 2022, cannot and does not
substantiate or support, sufficiently or at all, a reasonable suspicion of partiality on the part of the Chairperson.
78. As regards the alleged exclusion of the Appellant from the communications between the Board of Appeal and
the CPVO/Examination Office before the Oral Hearing, the Alternate Board note the following points.
79. First, and as regards the Board’s Technical Questions, communicated by the Registry to the CPVO and other
parties on 2 May 2022, the Board of Appeal notes, as a preliminary remark, that the Board of Appeal has a right to
investigate the facts and circumstances surrounding an appeal “of its own motion” (see, amongst others, Aurora Srl
v CPVO (T-140/15) [2017], ECLI:EU:T:2017:830, paras 72-74, 77 and Article 51 of the Proceedings Regulation and
Article 76 of the Basic Regulation) which includes the ability to raise relevant technical questions before an oral
hearing with the parties. At the same time, and without it being necessary to rule on the alleged infringement of
the principles of due process or right to a fair trial, an issue which can only, in principle, be decided before the EU
Courts, the Alternate Board notes that the communication of such questions should not disregard or undermine the
rights of parties to an appeal proceedings, or put them at a procedural disadvantage. Where the Board of Appeal
communicates relevant technical questions to one party in the appeal proceedings and there is no valid justification
for an undue delay in communicating the same questions to the other party in the appeal proceedings which puts
one of the party’s in a potentially procedurally advantageous position; where the questions are not provided in the
relevant language; and/or where the questions are provided to parties who are not party to the appeal proceedings,
without the prior knowledge of a party to the appeal proceedings - there are, in principle, legitimate grounds for
raising an objection pursuant to Article 48 of the Basic Regulation which may be sufficient to substantiate and
support the objection itself.
80. Second, and as regards the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, the Alternate Board notes that this document was
submitted by the CPVO to the Board of Appeal unrequested and without warning, i.e. as a ‘spontaneous submission’.
Having received this document from the CPVO on Friday 13 May 2022 at 17.59, the Board of Appeal disclosed this
document to the Appellant on Monday 16 May 2022 at 12.31. The Board of Appeal therefore disclosed this document
to the Appellant within 1 working day of its receipt. It is incumbent on the Board of Appeal to ensure that documents
received from parties to an appeal are admissible, can be added to the case file, and take any further action
(including the redaction of relevant confidential information) before disclosure to the other parties to the appeal.
This is particularly relevant in light of spontaneous submissions from parties which are unrequested and unforeseen
(see to that effect CPVO Board of Appeal Procedural Decision of 15 May 2012, Ralf Schräder v CPVO relating to
Variety denomination Sumost 02, paragraphs 50-59). The Alternate Board notes that 1 working-day to review the
CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, particularly in light of its length and complexity, and then communicate that
submission to the Appellant cannot be regarded as inconsistent with the principle of sound administration. The
Alternate Board also notes that, by the time the Appellant received the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, the Appellant
had already withdrawn its request for an Oral Hearing, and prevented the Oral Hearing from going ahead in practice
by, amongst other things, cancelling the ‘dry run’ which was necessary to ensure the videoconference line and
facilities functioned as required, before the Oral Hearing. Therefore, the Appellant’s submissions concerning the
communication of the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs “one day before the date of the Oral Hearing” and the inability
for the Appellant to prepare answers to the Board’s Technical Questions before the Oral Hearing – are of no material
weight or relevance – as the Oral Hearing had already been cancelled, and the Appellant had already ensured the
Oral Hearing could not, in practice, go-ahead, before the Board of Appeal provided the Appellant the CPVO’s
Response to the BTQs.
81. Third, the Alternate Board notes that no Oral Hearing was held on 16 May 2022, and no oral hearing has been
held in the appeal proceedings. The Alternate Board further notes that had an oral hearing taken place, the Appellant
cannot know with certainty what would, or would not, have happened, and whether and how the alleged procedural
deficiencies, and concerns regarding a fair trial, would have been addressed. The Appellant’s assertions that, for
example, the Oral Hearing was set to be held, and would have been held, in a manner “to surprise the Appellant”
on the substantive issues and not in accordance with the right to a fair trial, or in accordance with the equality of
arms – are merely suppositions, and cannot be sufficiently supported or substantiated by the facts.
11 / 13

82. Fourth, on the 16 May 2022 the Appellant lodged its Objection with the CPVO Board of Appeal. On 17 May 2022,
the Registry sent an email to the Appellant stating “[O]nly through your letter, the Board became aware of the fact
that the [Board’s Technical Questions] was not sent to you before. This has clearly been caused by a human error
for which the Board apologizes”. That email also proposed immediate corrective action, in particular, it included an
invitation for the Appellant to provide written observations responding to the Board’s Technical Questions, and the
CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, within 3 months. The Alternate Board therefore notes that, having become aware
of the potential mistake in not informing the Appellant of the Board’s Technical Questions, the Chairperson, as well
as the other members of the Board of Appeal, took immediate, decisive and proportionate corrective action and did
so in a transparent and clear manner. Moreover, the Alternate Board notes that it can find no reason why this
proposed corrective action does not address or remedy the alleged procedural defects earlier in the appeal
proceedings and/or why this action does not redress any procedural advantage the CPVO may have had earlier in
the appeal proceedings. Lastly, in this regard, the Alternate Board notes that the corrective action proposed and
taken by the Chairperson, and other members of the Board of Appeal, was similar, if not the same, as the corrective
action the Appellant itself had suggested and described in its Objection Letter. It therefore follows that the Appellant
cannot now take the view, that the corrective action taken is not sufficient or adequate to remedy the potential
procedural irregularities that occurred earlier in the process – or that by taking this action the facts substantiate or
support the view that a reasonable suspicion of partiality concerning the Chairperson arises.
83. Fifth, the Alternate Board notes the practical and legal consequences following the cancellation of the Oral
Hearing. In particular the Alternate Board notes that the CPVO and the Examination Office had from 2 May 2022
until 17 May 2022 (i.e. approximately 15 calendar days), to prepare oral submissions concerning the Board’s
Technical Questions. In contrast, the Appellant has been given, in total, from 17 May 2022 until 31 August 2022
(i.e. approximately 107 calendar days), to provide written observations on the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, and
the Board’s Technical Questions, in part due to the language versions provided. The Alternate Board therefore
concludes that the Appellant has not been put at any procedural disadvantage as regards, for example, its ability to
effectively make known its views on the Board’s Technical Questions and/or the CPVO’s Response to the BTQs, or
relating to the failure to notify the Appellant of the Board’s Technical Questions before the Oral Hearing scheduled
for 17 May 2022, which did not take place.
84. Given the above, the Alternate Board finds that, the events leading up to the Oral Hearing scheduled for 17 May
2022, when considered together and in particular in light of the corrective action taken by the Chairperson, and the
other members of the Board of Appeal, on 17 May 2022 and thereafter, cannot and do not substantiate or support,
sufficiently or at all, a reasonable suspicion of partiality on the part of the Chairperson.
85. In light of the above, the Alternate Board concludes that the Appellant’s second plea must therefore be
dismissed.
Third plea: According to the Appellant, even if the alleged infringement of the procedural rules are
rectified, the Chairperson must still be removed, as, following the conduct of the appeal proceedings
to-date, the Appellant cannot expect a fair trial under the Chairperson, and the Appellant’s suspicion
of partiality would continue to persist.
86. The Appellant asserts, that as the Appellant was, amongst other things, deprived of extensive and complex
information relevant to the appeal proceedings before the scheduled date of the Oral Hearing “the Appellant must
come to the conclusion that it cannot expect a fair trial under the Chairperson”. The Appellant states that, even if
the potential procedural flaws and deficiencies are addressed and rectified, it would not render the Objection itself
as null and void, as, “after all, even [if the infringement of the procedural rules are rectified] then the suspicion of
partiality persists”. The Appellant states that in order to ensure that the proceedings are conducted correctly in the
rule of law, the person responsible for complying with a rule of law procedure, “namely the chairperson of the Board
of Appeal” as a legally competent member “must therefore be removed”.
87. The CPVO rejects this plea and the related lines of argument.
Findings of the Board
88. The Alternate Board notes that where there are no facts or evidence which are capable of sufficiently
substantiating or supporting a reasonable suspicion of partiality, a partiality objection cannot be upheld. Merely
because a party in the appeal proceedings purports to have a suspicion of partiality, or purports to continue to have
a suspicion of partiality, does not mean that the necessary requirements, as set out in, amongst others, Article 48
12 / 13

of the Basic Regulation, are met. Moreover, and in any event, the Alternate Board notes that, according to the case-
law of the EPO Boards of Appeal, which may apply by analogy to the CPVO Board of Appeal, partiality objections
involving procedural deficiencies are generally only capable of supporting a decision to remove or reject a member
of the EPO Boards of Appeal, if they “result from…a preconceived attitude or deliberate intention” (See Case T
1257/14 of 5 February 2018, ECLI:EP:BA:2018:T125714.20180205). As the Alternate Board has already concluded,
the facts in this case are not capable of supporting or substantiating a reasonable suspicion of partiality. This is
particularly in light of the corrective action taken by the Board of Appeal on 17 May 2022 and thereafter, which the
Alternate Board considers transparent, decisive and proportionate. That action in particular, removes beyond doubt,
any possible suspicion of partiality vis-à-vis the Chairperson, in particular any possible suspicion that procedural
deficiencies were the result of a preconceived attitude or deliberate intention.
89. On the basis of the above, the Alternate Board concludes that the third plea is not well founded and must
therefore be dismissed.
VI. Decision as to the Action to be Taken:
90. The CPVO Board of Appeal, in its alternate composition, orders that:
- The Objection be dismissed.
- The Chairperson not be removed.
- In light of the Appellant’s withdrawal of its request for an oral hearing before being informed of all the necessary
facts and circumstances, the Alternate Board recommends that the parties in the appeal proceedings be invited to
attend an oral hearing, and an oral hearing be convened, should the parties and/or the Board of Appeal consider it
necessary. In the event an oral hearing is convened, the Alternate Board recommend that the parties be invited to
submit new pleading notes to assist the interpreters.
Marcus NAVIN-JONES Dirk REHEUL
Vice-Chairperson of the Board of Appeal Rapporteur
13 / 13

parties: Böhm-Nordkartoffel Agrarproduktion-GmbH & Co. OHG v CPVO
title: CPVO BoA A021/2021 - Vineta
text:
Appeal Case A021/2021
DECISION
of the Board of Appeal of 14 December 2022
Concerning the appeal lodged by
Böhm-Nordkartoffel Agrarproduktion-GmbH & Co. OHG
Postfach 1380
D-21303 Lüneburg, Germany
Represented by Mrs. S. Ahrens von Bismarck, Rechtsanwältin
Rothenbaumchaussee 7
D-20148 Hamburg, Germany
Appellant
against a decision of
Community Plant Variety Office
3 boulevard Maréchal Foch
CS 10121,
49101 ANGERS CEDEX 2, FRANCE
Represented by Ms. O. Lamberti, Legal Advisor
Other Party to the Proceedings,
Relating to Community Plant Variety Right No EU 0527
Variety denomination: Vineta
Species: Solanum Tuberosum L.
On 14 December 2022, the Board of Appeal of the Community Plant Variety Office, composed of Mr. P. van der
Kooij (Chairman), Mr. K. Riechenberg (Rapporteur) and Mrs. C. Negro (Member), gave the following decision:
1. The decision of the Community Plant Variety Office of 1st October 2021 (with reference
NG/20210088416) labelled “Re: Corrigendum” is annulled.
2. The Office is ordered to bear the costs of the Appellant, pursuant to Article 85(1) of Council
Regulation (EC) No. 2100/94.

I. SUMMARY OF FACTS AND PROCEEDINGS
1. On 15 August 1995, the Community Plant Variety Office (hereinafter “CPVO” or “Office”) received an
application for a Community Plant Variety Right (hereinafter “CPVR”) for the variety Vineta of the species
Solanum Tuberosum L. (application No. 1995/1013). On 2 August 1996, by Decision No. EU 0527, the CPVO
granted the right for said variety for a period expiring at the latest on 1st August 2026.
2. At the time of the Community grant the variety Vineta enjoyed national protection in Germany as of 3 March
1994.
3. By letter of 1st October 2021 (reference NG/20210088416), under the heading “Re: Corrigendum”, the Office
informed the Appellant that it had identified the following “discrepancies” regarding the expiry date of
protection recorded for the variety Vineta in the sense that (1.) the reduction of the duration of a national
protection at the date of granting the CPVR from the 30 year duration had been “miscalculated” and that (2.)
the period of protection should run until the last day of the year in question, as specified by Article 19 of
Council Regulation (EC) No. 2100/94 (hereinafter “basic regulation”).
4. In the same letter the Office indicated to the Appellant that it had made the following “corrections”, pursuant
to Article 53(4) of Commission Regulation (EC) No. 874/2009 (hereinafter “implementing regulation”), to Title
No. EU 0527 concerning the variety denomination Vineta: Expiry date of protection: Original 01/09/2026 –
New: 31/12/2024. The CPVO added to its letter an Extract of the Register of 1st October 2021 containing the
modification of the expiry date of protection for the variety at issue and invited the Appellant to contact the
Office as to any queries regarding the matter.
5. By e-mail of 5 October 2021, the Appellant asked the CPVO to indicate the legal basis upon which this decision
had been taken. As understood by the Appellant, according to Article 19 of the basic regulation the duration
of protection for potato varieties amounts to 30 years beginning with the calendar year following the grant of
the CPVR, so that the protection given to the Vineta variety should end at 31 December 2027.
6. By letter of reply of 7 October 2021, the Office explained that, given the national protection awarded to the
variety in question as from 3 March 1994, a reduction of the Community protection granted of two full years
“should have been made” pursuant to Article 1(2) of Council Regulation (EC) No. 2470/96 (hereinafter “potato
regulation”). The CPVO stressed in the same letter that in the case of varieties for which a national plant
variety right was awarded prior to the grant of the CPVR, but to which Article 116(4), fourth indent, of the
basic regulation does not apply, the extension referred to in Article 1(1) of the potato regulation shall be
reduced by the longest period in full years during which any national property right granted has been effective
in a Member State in respect of the same variety prior to the grant of the CPVR.
7. On 14 October 2021, the CPVO received a notice of appeal against the communication of 1st October 2021.
8. By date of 28 January 2022, the Appellant filed a written statement setting out the grounds of appeal and
applied for an interlocutory revision of the decision contained in the letter of the Office of 1st October 2021.
The Appellant requested the CPVO to revoke said decision and to reinstate the prior status of the CPVR.
9. On 24 February 2022, the Rectification Committee of the Office proceeded to the requested interlocutory
revision of the appeal. It decided not to rectify the contested decision and to remit the appeal to the Board of
Appeal. The Committee also held that the appeal has suspensory effect.
10. By letter dated 31 March 2022, the Appellant submitted comments on the interlocutory revision declaring to
“repeat the appeal filed against the decision” requesting that the latter “be revoked” and the prior status of
the CPVR “be reinstated”. In its letter the Appellant reiterated the positions taken in the grounds of appeal
and formulated further considerations concerning the admissibility of the appeal.
2 / 8

11. On 8 June 2022 the Board of Appeal invited the CPVO to submit its views thereto by 7 August 2022. The Office
responded by requesting an extension of this time limit to 8 September 2022. Such extension was granted by
the Board.
12. The observations of the CPVO were duly received by this date.
13. In its brief the Office indicated, as a “preliminary remark”, that the comments of the Appellant of 31 March
2022 “should not be considered validly filed” and not be taken into consideration, because the latter had not
been invited by the Board to do so.
14. At the hearing which, on 30th November 2022, was conducted by videoconference both parties reiterated in
substance the arguments brought forward in their written submissions.
15. The Appellant requests the Board to declare the appeal admissible and to determine that the decision taken
by the CPVO on 1st October 2021 was incorrect and shall thus be withdrawn by the Office reinstating the prior
status and duration of the CPVR for the variety Vineta until 1st August 2026.
16. The CPVO asks the Board to reject the appeal and rule that the fees pertaining to it shall not be reimbursed
to the Appellant.
II. SUMMARY OF ARGUMENTS OF THE PARTIES
17. The Appellant claims that the appeal is admissible and well-founded arguing that the contested decision is null
and void, for formal (procedural) and substantive reasons. Therefore, the initial decision establishing the CPVR
in question remains valid with regard to the expiry of this right as well as the corresponding entry in the CPVO
register.
18. As far as formal (procedural) aspects are concerned the Appellant observes first that, contrary to Article 75 of
the basic regulation and Article 18 of the European Code of Good Administrative Behaviour (hereinafter “EU
code”), the contested decision did not state the grounds it is based upon nor a proper reasoning so as to
enable its addressee to comprehend the factual and legal elements behind it, i.e. the recalculation of the
duration of protection relating to the Vineta variety. Nor had the Office offered the opportunity to present
comments regarding said decision.
19. Second, the Appellant stresses that, contrary to Article 53(3) of the implementing regulation and Article 19 of
the CPVO code, the contested decision was not accompanied by a statement specifying possible means of
appeal as well as the time limits for lodging such an appeal.
20. Third, the Appellant points out that, contrary to Article 16 of the CPVO code, the Office did not provide for the
opportunity to submit written comments and present them before the decision was taken.
21. As far as the substantive aspects of the case are concerned, the Appellant takes the position that the
amendment to the entry in the CPVO register at issue is a decision subject to an appeal pursuant to Article 67
of the basic regulation.
22. The Appellant recalls that the decision to be corrected in the sense of Article 53(4) of the implementing
regulation is the decision adopted by the CPVO to grant a CPVR for the potato variety Vineta in 1996, which
was to last until 2026. This decision was, at the time it was taken, properly registered and documented in the
corresponding certificate. No mistake, no linguistic error, no error of transcription, nor any other obvious
inaccuracy in the transmission of the technical information can be identified when the variety in question was
entered into the CPVO register.
23. The Appellant claims that the Office did not incur in a “patent mistake” when the CPVR at issue was granted,
but that its decision was of substantial nature in the legal sense. The concept of “patent mistake” in Article
3 / 8

53(4) of the implementing regulation is limited to obvious formal mistakes, as opposed to an error in the
calculation of the expiry date of a CPVR. The amendment to the certificate operated by the Office affects the
scope and the substance of the decision granting the CPVR in question, which comprises the period of
protection relating thereto.
24. The Appellant indicates that there is no legal basis for a withdrawal (even partial) of a CPVR due to an
administrative error made by the competent authority. The only available options for a valid withdrawal of a
CPVR are laid down in Articles 20 and 21 of the basic regulation. However, none of the conditions for such a
decision applies in the present case.
25. The Appellant contests the view taken by the Office in its decision of 24 February 2022 that the correction in
the CPVO Register was only due to a “plain human oversight” and that it is to be qualified as a mere correction
of a “clerical mistake” within the meaning of Article 53(4) of the implementing regulation. On the contrary, a
modification of the duration of a CPVR constitutes a material change to the initial decision granting the CPVR.
26. The Appellant also invokes the principles of protection of legitimate expectations and legal certainty,
emphasising that by revoking its initial decision of 1996 and replacing it with a new one in 2021, thereby
reducing the duration of protection of the CPVR in question by a period of about two years, the CPVO has
disregarded the binding nature of a definitive decision adopted by it previously. The title holder was in no way
responsible for the wrong calculation of the duration of said right and has relied upon the CPVR grant at issue
in good faith for over 25 years.
27. The Appellant concludes that the decision taken in 1996 by which legal protection was granted to the variety
Vineta can neither be revoked retroactively nor altered with future effect on the ground of a mistake or
miscalculation in the past.
28. The position of the Office appears in points 13 to 29 of the decision taken on 24 February 2022 by the
Rectification Committee as well as in its submissions to the Board of Appeal of 8 September 2022.
29. The CPVO emphasises in the first place that the Appellant had not been invited by the Board to provide
comments regarding the interlocutory revision adopted on 24 February 2022. It follows from a combined
reading of Articles 71(2) and 76 of the basic regulation that it is incumbent upon the Board to ask the parties
to furnish observations relating to the dispute pending before it and that, in the absence of a request thereto,
any brief filed should be disregarded.
30. According to the CPVO the appeal is not admissible, since the calculation of the CPVR duration, under the non-
transitional period, for the variety at issue is not a matter of legal interpretation, but an operation correcting a
“plain human oversight”. Such a “corrigendum of duration” adopted to rectify a “clerical mistake” cannot be
subject to an appeal according to Article 67 of the basic regulation which, due to the wording “shall lie”,
contains an exhaustive list of the decisions that can be subject to an appeal. While said provision refers to
decisions concerning entries to and cancellations in the CPVO register, it does not embrace amendments of
entries which may be realized in situations of “patent mistakes” according to Article 53(4) of the implementing
regulation.
31. Emphasising its position on the admissibility of the appeal, the Office explains that, since the variety at stake
was of the species Solanum Tuberosum L., its duration of protection was extended by five years pursuant to
the potato regulation which entered into force after the grant of the CPVR. However, said regulation also
provides for a reduction of this duration corresponding to the national protection already enjoyed by the variety
to be calculated in full years, resulting in the setting of the date of expiration on 31 December 2024. The
mistake made regarding said date should be qualified as not only “obvious and apparent”, but also as of a
“formal and not substantial nature” in the sense that it concerned a “numerical calculation” and not an
“assessment of substantial nature” affecting or reducing the scope of the right granted.
32. As regards the obligation to state grounds as required by Article 75 of the basic regulation, the CPVO considers
to have provided “concise and precise explanations of the calculations performed”.
4 / 8

33. The Office takes the view that, according to Article 53(3) of the implementing regulation, it is required to
indicate in any decision that an appeal is possible. However, this is the case only for an appealable decision
referred to in Article 67 of the basic regulation. In the present case no such decision has been adopted.
34. The CPVO underlines that the Appellant has not been deprived of the right to formulate comments. In fact
such right has been exercised.
35. As to the application of the transitional regime established by Article 116 of the basic regulation, the Office
argues that in the balance between the concept of legal certainty on the one hand and the principle of legality
of administrative decisions on the other the latter should prevail. The “legitimate interest” and the “individual
expectations” of the title holder cannot override the “public interest” in the maintenance of an “accurate and
reliable” register of exclusive rights.
36. The Office concludes therefore that the principle of legal certainty cannot justify the “reiteration of a mistake
committed in the past”. On the contrary, the CPVO must have the legal faculty to “open closed proceedings”
in order to rectify an incorrect element concerning the duration and expiration of a CPVR.
III. REASONS
On the objection raised by the Office against the submissions brought forward by the Appellant dated 31 March
2022
37. The Board of Appeal notes that while, according to Article 71(2) of the basic regulation, when examining the
appeal, the Board “shall as often as necessary invite the parties … to file observations on notifications issued
by itself or on communications from the other parties to the appeal proceedings …”, the unsolicited document
presented by the Appellant dated 31st March 2022 cannot be disregarded.
38. In fact, the Board has accepted the submissions of the Appellant by inviting the CPVO to comment upon them.
In exercising its discretion and in compliance with the principle of procedural economy, the Board considered
it unnecessary to invite the Appellant to file observations on the interlocutory revision adopted on 24 February
2022, given that such observations had already been spontaneously submitted by the Appellant. It would be
indeed inconsistent with a proper conduct of the proceedings before the Board to deprive the Appellant of the
opportunity to react in detail to the decision of the Rectification Committee of the Office and the numerous
legal developments contained therein.
39. The submissions presented by the Appellant dated 31st March 2022 are therefore held to be taken into account.
On the admissibility of the appeal
40. In view of the arguments brought forward by the Office the Board has to determine in the first place whether
the action introduced by the Appellant concerns a decision against which an appeal is available.
41. In the present case the communication of the CPVO dated 1st October 2021 and labelled “Re: Corrigendum”,
read together with the explanations given thereto by letter dated 7th October 2021, is to be regarded as the
administrative measure against which the appeal is directed.
42. The Office arguing that this communication cannot be subject to an appeal, it is necessary to examine the
legal nature of said document.
43. More precisely, the Board is called upon to evaluate whether the communication at issue is governed by Article
53(4) of the implementing regulation, stipulating that “linguistic errors, errors of transcription and patent
mistakes in decisions of the Office shall be corrected”. If this were the case, said communication could not be
5 / 8

qualified as an appealable decision. On the other hand, should Article 53(4) of this regulation not be applicable,
the Board has to determine whether the administrative act in question is nonetheless a decision subject to an
appeal.
44. Both parties have put forward divergent interpretations of this provision.
45. The Board recalls in this respect that the General Court in its judgment of 25 June 2020 (Siberia Oriental/CPVO,
case T-737/18, point 52; hereinafter “Siberia judgment”) has ruled that the “only legitimate purpose” of
corrections made on the basis of said provision is to correct “spelling mistakes or grammatical errors, errors
of transcription … or errors which are so obvious that nothing but the wording as corrected could have been
intended”. In addition, in point 53 of the same judgment, the General Court has underlined that the rule
allowing for such corrections “is to be interpreted strictly”.
46. Hence, a “mistake” or “error” in the sense of Article 53(4) of the implementing regulation must be of such
characteristics that it can be identified by a simple reading of the body of the decision itself. No such “mistake”
or “error” can be established on the basis of this provision when it is necessary to have recourse to statutory
interpretations of EU and national law as well as calculations of time limits relating to the specifics of the variety
concerned in order to identify an erroneous legal determination in the decision at issue.
47. The Board observes that the amendment to the Register operated by the CPVO relates to the scope and
substance of the CPVR validly granted in 1996 by reducing the duration of said right. Due to its material
consequence the measure taken by the Office must be qualified as a substantive decision which affects the
timely dimension of the right in question, the length of protection being an essential integral part of the latter.
This legal qualification cannot be circumvented by its labelling as a “corrigendum”. Also, allowing the CPVO to
amend the scope and substance of a CPVR by way of recourse to Article 53(4) of the implementing regulation
would deprive the holder of it of the faculty to have legal redress against such measure.
48. It follows that the above-mentioned provision is not applicable in the present case.
49. The CPVO argues nevertheless that the communication of 1st October 2021 is not covered by Article 67 of the
basic regulation and is therefore not amenable to an appeal.
50. The Board holds that this position cannot be sustained.
51. Indeed, Article 67 of the basic regulation, as indicated in its first paragraph, must be read in conjunction with
its Article 87 as far as “the entering or deletion of information in the Register” is concerned (Siberia judgment,
point 36). In this regard, Article 87(2), letter e, stipulates that the CPVO Register shall comprise “the date on
which the Community plant variety right begins and ends, together with the reasons for the termination of
right”. The amendment of the expiry date of the CPVR amounts to “entering of information in the Register” as
regards “the date on which the Community plant variety right ends” in accordance with Articles 67 and 87(2),
letter e of the basic regulation.
52. As outlined in paragraph 47 of the present decision, the administrative act under examination has produced
legal effects upon the CPVR validly granted and held by the Appellant.
53. The Board thus considers that, on proper interpretation of Articles 67 and 87 of the basic regulation, the
measure adopted by the Office constitutes a decision against which an appeal must be allowed. Otherwise,
the Appellant would be deprived of a legal remedy against a decision concerning the CPVR granted to its
holder.
54. Indeed, the principle of effective judicial review mandates that no administrative act adopted in the field of
application of EU law having legal effects can escape review by the competent judicial or quasi-judicial
authority. The European Court of Justice has underlined the overriding importance of said principle on multiple
occasions, in particular in its judgments of 23 April 1986 (Les Verts/European Parliament, case 294/83, ECR
p.1339, points 23 to 25), of 15 May 1986 (Johnston, case 222/84, ECR p.1651, point 18), of 15 October 1987
6 / 8

(Heylens, case 222/86, ECR p.4112, point 14) and of 3 December 1992 (Borelli/Commission, case C-97/91,
ECR p.I-6313, point 14).
55. It follows from this jurisprudence that in the present dispute an appeal must be allowed, the contested
amendment to the Register having produced precise detrimental effects upon the legal position held by the
Appellant.
56. The appeal, having been introduced in due form and time, is therefore admissible.
On the substance of the appeal
57. It is appropriate to examine first the substantive arguments put forward by the Appellant (paragraphs 21 to
27 of the present decision).
58. The Board observes that there is no provision in the basic regulation allowing the Office to alter the content
of a CPVR validly granted, such as the length of protection contained therein.
59. Given this absence of a statutory basis for such a substantive modification of the right concerned, the Office
must establish that a general principle of law enables it to adopt a measure reducing the duration of a CPVR.
60. In this regard the CPVO has argued that the “public interest” in the existence of a correct Register constitutes
such a general principle of law and a legal basis to withdraw in part the protection granted by the initial
decision.
61. The Board emphasises that, supposing such “public interest” is to be recognised, said principle must be
balanced against other general principles of law the Appellant may rely upon, such as the concept of legal
certainty, the protection of a validly acquired CPVR by way of an administrative decision having become final
as well as the recognition of legitimate expectations of the title holder generated by such a decision, such as
those based upon the duration of the right in question.
62. It also must be underlined that the erroneous calculation of the duration of the CPVR validly awarded occurred
more than twenty years ago without having been detected by the competent administrative unit of the CPVO
and could in no way be attributed to misinformation or wrongful statements made by the Appellant in the
context of the application for protection of the variety at issue.
63. The Board recalls that legal certainty is one of a number of general principles recognised by EU law (Siberia
judgment, point 34).
64. The Board finds that the contested amendment to the Register has the effect of undermining the binding
nature of the definitive decision granting the CPVR in question in the sense of the considerations contained in
point 53 of this judgment of the General Court. This measure must therefore be regarded as being incompatible
with the principle of legal certainty.
65. In view of these particular circumstances which characterize the present dispute the Board is of the opinion
that the Office has failed to demonstrate that the alleged “public interest” should prevail over the general legal
principles relied upon by the Appellant as indicated in paragraph 61 of the present decision.
66. Given this appreciation it is not necessary to evaluate the arguments raised by the Appellant relating to
procedural (formal) aspects of the proceedings before the Office (paragraphs 18 to 20 of the present decision).
67. It follows that the decision adopted by the CPVO on 1st October 2021, labelled “Re: Corrigendum” is invalid.
7 / 8

IV. CONCLUSION
68. Said decision must therefore be annulled.
V. ON THE COSTS
69. According to Article 85(1) of the basic regulation, the losing party to appeal proceedings shall bear the costs
incurred by the other party to the proceedings. The Appellant having prevailed in its submissions, the Office
is ordered to bear said costs.
VI. ON LEGAL REMEDIES
70. Pursuant to Article 73 of the basic regulation an action may be brought before the Court of Justice against this
decision within two months of its service.
Paul VAN DER KOOIJ Kurt RIECHENBERG
Chairman of the Board of Appeal Rapporteur
8 / 8

parties: Eurosemillas S.A. v CPVO, Nadorcott S.A.R.L., Carpa Dorada S.L.
title: CPVO BoA A002/2020 - 'Nadorcott'
text:
Appeal Case A002/2020
DECISION
of the Board of Appeal of 2 January 2023
Concerning the appeal lodged by
Eurosemillas, SA
Paseo de la Victoria, 31, 14004 Córdoba (Spain)
Represented by Mr. J. Muñoz-Delgado y Mérida
Paseo de la Castellana, nº 216, 28046 Madrid (Spain)
Appellant
Other parties to the appeal procedure:
Nadorcott Protection S.A.R.L.
51 rue Jules Barbier, Le Stanislas, 83700 Saint-Raphaël (France)
Represented by Ms. I. Pi i Amorós
Príncipe de Vergara, 187, Plaza de Rodrigo Uría, 28002 Madrid (Spain)
Title holder
and
Carpa Dorada, S.L.
C/Manuel Vivanco, 12, 12005 Almazora (Spain)
Represented by Ms. I. Pérez-Cabrero-Fernández
Plaza del Ayuntamiento, 29, 46002 Valencia (Spain)
Intervener
vs.
Community Plant Variety Office
3 boulevard Maréchal Foch, CS 10121,49101 Angers Cedes 2 (France)
Represented by Ms. M. García-Moncó Fuente
Defendant
Relating to Community Plant Variety Right No EU 14111
Variety denomination: Nadorcott
Species: Citrus reticulata Blanco
On 2 January 2023 the Board of Appeal of the Community Plant Variety Office, composed of P. van der Kooij
(Chairman), S. Martin (Rapporteur) and H. Ghijsen (Member), gave the following decision:
1. The appeal is admissible but not well-founded and is therefore dismissed.
2. Decision No. NN 20 is upheld.
3. The costs of the appeal proceedings shall be borne by the Appellant, pursuant to Article
85 (1) of Council Regulation No. 2100/94.

I. SUMMARY OF THE FACTS
a. The development of the variety ‘Nadorcott’
1. In 1963-64 trees of the ‘Murcott’ variety were planted in several plots of the Institut National de la Recherche
Agronomique (INRA) of Morocco, among them one in the town of Afourer.
2. In 1981-82, the INRA researcher, Mr. Nadori, found in the seedling population originating from the ‘Murcott’
variety, planted in 1963/64, the original tree of the new variety encoded as INRA 21 W. This tree, apparently
a cross between ‘Murcott’ and an unknown pollinizer, drew his attention since its fruit showed a better
coloration, easy peeling and less seeds, all characteristics highly appreciated for its commercial interest.
3. Between 1982 and 1983, INRA 21 W grafts were sent to Société des Services Agricoles au Maroc (SASMA) –
a body that included farmers in the citrus sector in Morocco- under the name INRA W in order to perform
behaviour tests. Accordingly, between 1983-84, SASMA distributed buds of INRA 21 W to farmers in different
regions to observe their behaviour. But the experiment was not successful: the trees produced fruit with an
excessive number of seeds so the variety was not considered to be of interest and therefore the trees were
removed by the farmers in 1985.
4. In 1988, Mr. Nadori identified on the Domaines Agricoles estate of Dar Es Salam five-years old INRA W
trees initially planted under the name ‘Murcott SASMA’ that were later re-named ‘Afourer’ at his request
to make allusion to its origin and to avoid confusion with the variety ‘Murcott’.
5. During the spring of 1988 Mr Nadori noticed that while some green-yellowish fruits of those trees (a result
of out-of-season flowering) did not have seeds, those with an orange-pink tone had many.
6. In 1989, Mr Nadori covered ‘Afourer’ trees from Dar Es Salam together with the INRA 21 W tree at Afourer’s
INRA testing station with an anti-insect net before the flowering period. The trees covered produced
seedless fruits while the uncovered trees had many seeds. Mr. Nadori thus proved that the INRA 21 W -
Afourer variety is self-incompatible.
7. In September 1989, Mr. Nadori informed both Domaines Agricoles and INRA of his discovery. He also
informed INRA of the need to start experimental plots for an assessment of the ‘Afourer’ variety on the
market.
8. Based on such request, between 1990 and 1991, an experimental plot was carried out in Morocco, in a
locality without citrus trees. In said plot, it was found that the new variety had no seeds only when cross-
pollination was prevented. New experimental plots were subsequently developed.
b. Filing of an application for registration of Community plant variety rights for the
variety ‘Nadorcott’
9. On 22 August 1995, Mr Jean De Maistre submitted to the Community Plant Variety Office (hereinafter also
referred to as ‘the Office’) an application for registration of Community plant variety rights for the variety
‘Nadorcott’ of the botanical taxon Citrus reticulata Blanco (Application number 1995/0726).
10. On 21 March 1997, Mr. De Maistre informed the Office of the transfer of all his rights concerning the
‘Nadorcott’ variety to Nadorcott Protection S.A.R.L. (NCP), its current owner.
11. On 4 October 2004, the Office granted the Community Plant Variety Right (CPVR) for the plant variety
‘Nadorcott’ (Registration No. EU 14111).
12. The registration of the grant was published in the Official Journal of the Office of 15 December 2004.
c. The first application for annulment
13. On 11 February 2005, the Valencian Federation of Agricultural Cooperatives (FECOAV) lodged an appeal
against that decision.
14. The application was rejected by a decision of the Board of Appeal of 8 November 2005 (Decision
A001/2005).
15. The decision was confirmed by the General Court (31/01/2008, T-95/06, EU:T:2008:25).
2 / 18

d. The second application for annulment
16. On 31 May 2016, the Office received an application for annulment of the CPVR for ‘Nadorcott’ (hereinafter
referred to as the “Request for annulment”) by Eurosemillas SA (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Appellant’
or ‘Eurosemillas/Euroseeds’).
17. The Request for annulment is based on Article 20(1)(a) and (c) of Council Regulation (EC) No. 2100/94 of
27 July 1994 on Community plant variety rights (hereinafter also referred to as the ‘Basic Regulation’ or
‘BR’).
18. Essentially, the Appellant alleges a lack of entitlement and a lack of novelty of the ‘Nadorcott’ plant variety
resulting from its commercialisation, albeit under the denomination ‘Afourer’, prior to 1980 in the territory
of the European Union.
19. On 6 June 2016, the Request for annulment was transmitted by the Office to the owner of the plant variety
‘Nadorcott’.
20. On 2 August 2016 the Office received a request from Carpa Dorada, SL (hereinafter ‘the interested party’
or ‘Carpa Dorada’) to be considered a party to the nullity proceedings.
21. The request was granted on 5 August 2016.
22. On 14 December 2016, the owner and the interested party filed their observations and comments to the
Request for annulment.
23. On 8 March 2017, the Appellant formally requested the Office, on the basis of the right to be heard under
Article 56(2) Proceedings Regulation No 874/2009 (‘Implementing Rules’ or ‘PR’), to be given three months
to submit observations in response to the pleadings of the other two parties.
24. On 13 March 2027, the Office granted said request.
25. On 9 June 2017, the Office received the response from the Appellant to the observations and comments
filed by the owner and the interested party (hereinafter referred to as the ‘responses’).
26. On 20 March 2018, the Office received the observations of the owner and the interested party to the
responses.
e. The contested decision
27. On 16 December 2019, the Office issued Decision No. NN 20 rejecting the request for annulment
(hereinafter referred to as the ‘Contested decision’).
f. The present proceedings
28. On 15 January 2020 the Appellant filed an appeal against the Contested decision, followed on 21 April
2020 by its Statement of grounds (hereinafter also the ‘SOG’).
29. On 15 December 2020, the Office filed its observations in reply to the statement of grounds.
g. The hearing
30. The oral hearing took place on 3 October 2022 in Angers, France. The hearing was attended by all parties
to the proceedings duly represented.
II. REASONS
On the admissibility of the appeal
31. The appeal complies with Articles 67, 68 and 69 BR. It is therefore admissible.
3 / 18

On the substance
1. Preliminary remarks
32. The Appellant raises nine grounds of appeal which will be addressed in the order proposed by the
Appellant.
33. However, before entering into the examination of the merits of the present appeal, the Board recalls that
the Office enjoys “a wide discretion concerning annulment of a plant variety right for the purposes of
Article 20 of Regulation No 2100/94, in so far as the protected variety underwent the examination set out
in the previous paragraph” (21 May 2015, C-546/12P, Lemon Symphony II, EU:C:2015:332, § 56).
34. As a result it is “only where there are serious doubts that the conditions laid down in Articles 7 or 10 of
that regulation had been met on the date of the examination provided for under Articles 54 and 55 of that
regulation can a re-examination of the protected variety by way of nullity proceedings under Article 20 of
Regulation No 2100/94 be justified” ((21 May 2015, C-546/12P, Lemon Symphony II, EU:C:2015:332, §
56).
35. As outlined by the Court of Justice, the burden of proof lies with the moving party, the Appellant in the
present case: “In that context, a third party seeking annulment of a plant variety right must adduce
evidence and facts of sufficient substance to raise serious doubts as to the legality of the grant of a plant
variety right following the examination provided for in Articles 54 and 55 of that regulation (21 May 2015,
C-546/12P, Lemon Symphony II, EU:C:2015:332, § 57).
36. This principle is now enshrined in article 53(a) PR as regards proceedings before the Community Plant
Variety Office which provides that “2. A request to the Office to open the proceedings on nullity or
cancellation, as referred to in Articles 20 and 21, respectively, of the basic regulation, shall be accompanied
by evidence and facts raising serious doubts as to the validity”.
37. This being said, the Board notices that the ‘Nadorcott’ variety which is the object of the present appeal
has already been examined by the Office on three different occasions: (1) in the course of the examination
procedure; (2) in the context of the appeal filed by the Federation of Agricultural Cooperatives of the
Valencian Community (FECOAV) on 18 April 2005; (3) in the course of the present annulment procedure.
Following these in-depth and complex examinations, the Office confirmed the validity of the plant variety
right granted to ‘Nadorcott’.
2. First ground of appeal: The alleged Violation of the fundamental right to good administration,
effective judicial protection and a the right to a fair trial resulting from the alleged breach by
the Office of its duty to investigate facts on its own motion in the course of the invalidity
proceedings
38. The Appellant submits that the Office failed (1) to properly investigate the matter in the course of the
examination proceedings and subsequently in the course of the invalidity proceedings; (2) to request the
appearance of witnesses as proposed by the Appellant; (3) to commission an expert report; (4) to order
the production of relevant documents in the hand of the parties or third parties.
39. Before entering into the merits of this first claim, it is useful to recall the relevant principles regarding the
burden of proof in invalidity proceedings.
2.1 Burden of proof in invalidity proceedings
40. In invalidity proceedings the burden of proof lies with the requesting party. That obligation stems from
Article 53a PR and the case-law of the General Court and the Court of Justice (21 May 2015,
Schräder/OCVV, C‑546/12 P, EU:C:2015:332, §57; 23 November 2017, M 02205, T‑140/15,
EU:T:2017:830, § 58)
41. The Appellant submits that its burden of proof is limited to prima facie evidence that there are serious
doubts about the validity of the Community protection. Once the nullity application is admitted the burden
of proof would shift to the Office who would be required to carry out an investigation of the facts and
evidence to the full satisfaction of the applicant, pursuant to Articles 76 and 60 BR.
42. The Board does not share that position. The initial admission of an application for nullity means that the
Office is satisfied that prima facie there are grounds for examining in detail the materials submitted in the
4 / 18

nullity application and to initiate inter partes proceedings. But it does not imply that the burden of proof
shifts towards the Office and the owner. It also does not imply that the Office is required to conduct
investigations pursuant to the wishes and desires of the Appellant.
2.2 The right of the Office to conduct measures of instruction and investigations must be
reconciled with the principle of “equality of arms”
43. The Board emphasizes that Invalidity proceedings are by definition inter partes proceedings in the course
of which the Office shall remain impartial in accordance with the principle of equality of arms which is part
of EU Law (19 May 2021, T-510/19, DEVICE OF A Jumping ANIMAL (fig.)/Puma (fig.) et al.,
EU:T:2021:281, § 70).
44. In invalidity proceedings the burden of proof lies with the parties (21 May 2015, Schräder/OCVV, C‑546/12
P, EU:C:2015:332, §57; 23 November 2017, M 02205, T‑140/15, EU:T:2017:830, § 58). In view of its
obligation to remain impartial the Office shall not conduct investigations of facts on its own volition.
45. The Board acknowledges that it is bound by the principle of sound administration, which requires it to
examine carefully and impartially all the relevant facts of a case and to obtain all the elements of law and
of fact necessary for the exercise of its discretion (19 December 2012, Brookfield New Zealand and Elaris
v CPVO and Schniga, C-534/10 P, EU: C: 2012: 813, par. 51; 8 June 2017, Schniga v CPVO, C-625/15
P, EU: C: 2017: 435, par. 47; 11 April 2019, Kiku GmbH, T-765/17, EU: T: 2019: 244, par. 41; 23
November 2017, T-140/15, Aurora/OCVV-SVanderhave (M 02205), EU: T: 2017: 830, par. 73).
46. Article 76 BR is an expression of the duty of sound administration, enshrined in Article 41 of the Charter
of Fundamental Rights, which entails the duty of the competent institution to examine carefully and
impartially all the relevant aspects of the individual case. It also requires the Board of Appeal to examine
carefully and impartially all the relevant facts and law of the case provided that they have been adduced
by the parties (11 April 2019, T-765/17, Kiku GmbH, EU:T:2019:244, §32).
47. It does not imply that the Office is required to initiate investigations to clarify and possibly to support the
arguments raised by one party. In that regard, it is apparent from the case-law that the Office cannot be
required to carry out further investigations where it considers that the preliminary investigation of the case
has been sufficient (Case 9/83 Eisen und Metall v Commission [1984] ECR 2071, paragraph 32, and Case
T‑141/94 Thyssen Stahl v Commission [1999] ECR II‑347, paragraph 110).
48. In the present case, the Office, after analysing the submissions and evidence of all parties, came to the
conclusion that it had gathered all necessary evidence. It was therefore entitled to reject the various
requests presented by the Appellant. This decision does not amount to arbitrariness (18 September 2012,
T-133/08, Schräder §§136-141).
2.3 The alleged failure of the Office to investigate the matter
49. The Appellant declares in its application that it has “no more evidence to present” but that relevant
information and documents are in the possession and under the control of NCP and under the exclusive
control of its members, the INRA and Domaines Agricoles.
50. The Appellant therefore asked the Office to conduct an investigation and to request the production of
documents regarding the following issues:
1. The identity of the ‘Nadorcott’ variety with the ‘Afourer’ variety.
2. The timing, the circumstances and the persons and entities that actually took part in the alleged
discovery and development of the mandarin variety INRA 21 W — Murcott/Afourer.
3. The nature, extent and dates of the different acts of disposal of components of the variety carried out
by Mr Nadori prior to the relevant grace period;
(a) The cultivation in Morocco and the export to the European Union of fruit of the mandarin variety, then
known as ‘Afourer’, prior to its alleged discovery by Mr Nadori at INRA’s premises in 1981.
(b) The transfer of propagating material from ‘Afourer’ to Moroccan producers, and in particular to the
Domaines Agricoles, carried out in 1982/83 by INRA, directly or via the SASMA nurseries.
(c) The marketing in Morocco of fruit of the harvest of plantations carried out by those Moroccan producers
on the basis of the propagating material referred to in the previous paragraph.
5 / 18

(d) The use by Domaines Agricoles of the propagating material in Morocco, the marketing of the fruit of
the variety in Morocco, the marketing of the fruit of the harvest, the conservation of at least 7 of those
trees in the Dar Es Salam plant, the use of propagating material obtained from these trees for the
production of village plantations in different locations, particularly planting 200 hectares in Agafay and
exporting the fruits of the harvest of those plantations to the European Union at the time of October 1988
or 22 August 1994.
(e) The transfer of propagating material from ‘Afourer’ to UCR (University of California Riverside, a US
Institute of research) carried out in 1984 and 1985 by Mr Nadori with the authorisation of INRA, its
subsequent addition to the Collection of UCR; its release into California nurseries and its bringing into
production and marketing by the growers in that State.
(f) The transfer of propagating material from ‘Afourer’ to the Spanish producer, Mr Boronat Flores, carried
out by Domaines Agricoles in 1988, its subsequent supply of propagating material to Spanish growers and
the production by those plantations of ‘Afourer’ and marketing of the fruits of the harvest in Spain from
1990 onwards.
(g) The exportation by Moroccan producers to the European Union of ‘Afourer’ fruit prior to 22 August
1994.
4. The circumstances relating to the negotiation and content of the agreements possibly reached between

3. Second ground of appeal: the Nadorcott variety was discovered and not developed
93. The Appellant argues that the 'Nadorcott' variety was discovered without further development thereafter
so that it would not have been the subject of ‘breeding’ and therefore not subject to protection.
94. The burden of proof that the ‘Nadorcott’ variety was discovered and not developed lies with the Appellant.
95. Article 1 of the 1991 UPOV Convention provides that “(iv) “breeder” means - the person who bred, or
discovered and developed, a variety”. The use of the word “or” clearly indicates that a new and protectable
variety can be the result of breeding or of a discovery and development.
96. The notion of “discovery” describes the activity of “selection within natural variation” while “development”
describes the process of “propagation and evaluation” of the variety discovered (UPOV Document C
(Extr.)/19/2/, point 16, the “2002 Document”).
97. The Appellant argues that the Office makes an interpretation of the concept of development which is
contrary to the interpretation given by UPOV.
98. To this end, the Appellant undertakes a detailed study of the work on the elaboration of the 2002
Document and the Explanatory Notes on the definition of breeder under the 1991 Act of the UPOV
Convention, Document UPOV/EXN/BRD of 2013.
99. The Appellant argues that the UPOV explanatory notes Document UPOV/EXN/BRD/1 (the “2013
Document”), has changed the position of UPOV on the concept of discovery and development previously
set out in the “2002 Document” and excludes from protection those varieties discovered which were
subject to “unchanged” multiplication.
100. The Board does not agree. First, the amendments made in 2013 are irrelevant since the contested
application for registration of Community plant variety rights for the variety ‘Nadorcott’ of the botanical
taxon Citrus reticulata Blanco (Application number 1995/0726) was filed in 1995.
101. For the sake of completeness, the Board notes that while it is true that the 2013 Document added the
phrase “a person shall not be entitled to obtain the protection of an existing variety that has been
discovered and reproduced unchanged”, the purpose of that addition is to avoid the protection of mere
findings made by people who discover a variety already cultivated in nature or a population of plant
material that has already been reproduced and is being cultivated, without performing any selection or
evaluation work, limiting the applicant to reproduce it without change, precisely because this does not
meet the ultimate purpose pursued by the UPOV, which is to contribute to the development of agriculture
with the creation and dissemination of new improved varieties.
102. The Board is of the view that, as mentioned in the article of Mr. Nadori, referred to in paragraph 145
below, the ‘Nadorcott’ variety was subject to breeding and development, including crossing, selection,
multiplication and evaluation of the variety. The variety originates from seedlings grown from seeds of the
variety ‘Murcott’. The “discovery” of the variety in 1981-82 by Mr. Nadori is an act of selection in a
population created by the breeder.
103. After becoming aware in 1988 of its self-incompatibility, the existence of which the Appellant does not
dispute, the ats performed by Mr. Nadori can be qualified as acts of development of the ‘Nadorcott’ variety.
The experimentation initiated and conducted by Mr Nadori led to the development of a set of processes
necessary to obtain a fruit without seeds.
104. The second ground of appeal is therefore rejected.

5. Fourth ground of appeal: lack of entitlement to file an application for a Community plant
variety right since the developer is citizen of the Kingdom of Morocco
122. The Appellant submits that since the Kingdom of Morocco was not member of UPOV, Mr. Nadori, a
Moroccan citizen, was not legally entitled to file an application for the protection of the ‘Nadorcott’ variety
in the European Community.
123. Article 12 BR as in force in 1994 provided for:
Entitlement to file an application for a Community plant variety right
An application for a Community plant variety right may be filed by any natural or legal person, or any body
ranking as a legal person under the law applicable to that body, provided they are: (a) nationals of one of
the Member States or nationals of a member of the Union for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants
within the meaning of Article 1 (xi) of the Act of 1991 of the International Convention for the Protection
of New Varieties of Plants, or are domiciled or have their seat or an establishment in such a State;(…).
124. The application was filed by Mr De Maistre who, as a French citizen, was undoubtedly entitled to file the
application.
125. The Board further endorses the conclusion of the contested decision that one should not confuse the issue
of entitlement to the protection (Article 11 BR) and the entitlement to file the application (Article 12 BR).
126. The entitlement to Community protection is substantive in nature and is regulated in Article 11 BR. This
status is held by anyone who breeds, or discovers and develops, a variety, as well as by his successors in
title. Article 11 BR does not establish any nationality requirement.
127. On the other hand, the entitlement to file applications under Article 12 BR is a procedural right,
independent of the right to variety protection, and relates only to the question who can be an applicant
for a variety right; this applicant does not necessarily have to be the breeder.
128. The BR does not require the breeder and the applicant to be the same person; nor does it state that the
breeder must have the capacity to file the application in order for an application filed by an assignee of its
rights (with capacity) to be valid. In fact, Regulation No. 15/2008, which removed the nationality
requirement for the entitlement to file applications, specifies in its Recital 2, that this reform was intended
to simplify the procedure, and that one application system for all applicants should be introduced.
129. The fourth ground of appeal is therefore rejected.

130. Article 10 BR provides that:
“1. A variety shall be deemed to be new if, at the date of application determined pursuant to Article 51,
variety constituents or harvested material of the variety have not been sold or otherwise disposed of to

others, by or with the consent of the breeder within the meaning of Article 11, for purposes of exploitation
of the variety:
(a) earlier than one year before the abovementioned date, within the territory of the Community;
(b) earlier than four years or, in the case of trees or of vines, earlier than six years before the said date,
outside the territory of the Community.
2. The disposal of variety constituents to an official body for statutory purposes, or to others on the basis
of a contractual or other legal relationship solely for production, reproduction, multiplication, conditioning
or storage, shall not be deemed to be a disposal to others within the meaning of paragraph 1, provided
that the breeder preserves the exclusive right of disposal of these and other variety constituents, and no

territory of the Community for purposes of exploitation of the variety, earlier than four years, in the case
of trees or of vines earlier than six years, before the entry into force of this Regulation, if the date of
application is within one year of that date.”
